meeting_header: Date: 2025-03-05 15:00 PST; Duration: 42m; Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), José Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Maple Financial), Ethan Cole (Maple Financial), Liam O'Neill (Maple Financial)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results comparing Redwood serving runtime vs customer baseline provider. Discussed latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput, batching and KV cache tuning, quantization tradeoffs, and next steps for tail-latency analysis and additional throughput runs. Action items assigned for spreadsheet handoff, sample data, and further SE runs.
topics: Benchmark results: latency & throughput vs baseline
Batching/KV cache tuning and config used
Operational notes: autoscaling, NUMA, GPU placement
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, looks like we've got about 40 minutes, we'll run through the benchmark summary then talk tuning and next steps. 
[00:12] Priya Singh: Great, thanks Maya. We reviewed the initial sheet you sent, appreciate the detail. Quick callout: we care about tail latency, p99, for interactive workflows. 
[00:25] José Alvarez: Yep understood. We ran three main families: hosted baseline (vendor A), customers baseline self-host, and our Redwood dedicated config with 8xA100 + kv cache and quantized int8. 
[00:40] Ethan Cole: One clarifying Q - the baseline numbers, were those identical request shapes? We saw some variance on token lengths. 
[00:52] José Alvarez: Good question. We matched seq lengths to your sample distribution that Priya shared last week, mean 128 tokens, 95th ~320. There is some jitter, transcription note: sequence vs sequeue, you know how the auto transcript sometimes swaps words. 
[01:06] Liam O'Neill: I'm mainly watching the p99. The sheet shows Redwood p99 ~ 420ms vs baseline 350ms in the hosted comparison, is that right? 
[01:18] Maya Chen: That's right for the hosted comparison w/ our default batching. The thing to flag is throughput at the same time: Redwood sustained 3.2k tokens/sec vs baseline 900 tokens/sec on similar GPU counts for the same cost bucket — so you trade tail-latency for much higher aggregate throughput. 
[01:34] Priya Singh: Hmm ok so throughput is better but tail is worse. For our app we need p99 < 400ms for interactive token-by-token. 
[01:44] José Alvarez: We have a few knobs. First, reduce batch delay and max batch size, that'll lower p99 but reduce throughput. Second, enable more aggressive kv caching for repeated prefixes — that cuts compute per request. Third, change model variant to smaller context-optimized variant. 
[02:03] Ethan Cole: Can you explain the KV cache setting? Our engineers saw a phrase 'KV cash' in the export and were confused. 
[02:12] José Alvarez: (laughs) Yes the transcript autocorrects. KV cache is the attention key/value cache; it avoids recomputing prefixes for chat-like workloads. When enabled and warmed, effective latency drops a lot on repeated prompts, especially for long context. 
[02:27] Priya Singh: Did you run runs with and without kv caching? The sheet shows both but not sure which rows correspond. 
[02:34] Maya Chen: We labeled them, but I agree it was a bit messy. We'll re-export with clearer column headers. The short answer: with kv cache enabled p95 improved from ~230ms to ~160ms, p99 from ~420ms to ~290ms in our dedicated config. 
[02:50] Liam O'Neill: Wait, p99 290ms? That would meet our target. Which config was that again? 
[02:55] José Alvarez: Dedicated Redwood with kv cache + smaller batching (b=4) and quantized int8 model. There's always a small accuracy delta with int8, we measured ~0.6% drop on your eval set, within your tolerance. 
[03:10] Priya Singh: That's encouraging. We do have strict correctness checks on named-entity extraction; can you share per-example diffs? 
[03:20] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include a per-example evaluation export. We'll redact PII from the sample set. 
[03:27] Ethan Cole: Regarding throughput, you said 3.2k tokens/sec sustained. Under what concurrency? 
[03:33] José Alvarez: That was sustained at 64 concurrent streams across the pool with batching enabled and our autoscaler configured to keep tails smooth. Again that's the tradeoff: to get throughput we batch more which can harm p99. 
[03:46] Priya Singh: Can Redwood do priority routing so critical interactive requests bypass big batches? 
[03:51] José Alvarez: Yes, we can set low-latency QoS routes that pin requests to smaller batch lanes; it's part of the smart routing policies. That will increase cost a bit but achieves p99 targets. 
[04:05] Liam O'Neill: On the infra side we need more detail on NUMA placement and GPU saturation. Your note mentioned shaders — I think you meant kernels. 
[04:15] José Alvarez: Right, kernel selection, my bad. For the throughput runs we tuned CUDA kernels and NUMA so the model shards are colocated to avoid cross-socket traffic. We'll share the runbook with the exact env flags and docker args. 
[04:30] Maya Chen: Action item: SE to share runbook link and exact commands. 
[04:35] Priya Singh: Also curious about multi-tenant noise; baseline single-tenant vs Redwood multi-tenant results? 
[04:43] José Alvarez: The tests included both dedicated and hosted multi-tenant modes. The row you flagged was dedicated. The hosted multi-tenant baseline had lower cost but had higher variance in tails. 
[04:57] Ethan Cole: For the dedicated pricing, is that a separate reserved pool? How much capacity would we need for 99th percentile throughput of our peak 200 RPS? 
[05:07] Maya Chen: Based on your sample distribution, estimated committed GPUs would be in the 4-6 A100 range to hit sustained 200 RPS interactive with p95 targets if we adopt small batches and kv cache. We'll send a capacity/price estimate in the updated sheet. 
[05:25] Priya Singh: Can we talk about quantization again — you mentioned 0.6% accuracy drop. What's the measurement method? 
[05:32] José Alvarez: We ran your eval prompt set — the classification metrics and NER precision recall — side-by-side. Quantized int8 gave slight differences in tokenization scoring and a few NER misses; full precision FP16 had the cleanest results but cost more. We'll include the per-prompt diffs. 
[05:48] Liam O'Neill: Any security concerns with kv cache and private context? We can't leak user data between tenants. 
[05:54] Maya Chen: KV cache is per-request and isolated per customer; in Dedicated we also offer tenant isolation and customer-managed KMS for keys, plus audit logs. We'll attach the security summary PDF and SOC2 reference. 
[06:08] Priya Singh: Good. One more ops question: how reproducible are the runs? We saw run-to-run variance on p99 ~30-50ms. 
[06:17] José Alvarez: There is some jitter from background system noise; we can rerun longer to get better confidence intervals. For p99 we recommend 10k+ requests per config. We'll run another long-run for the config that met p99 with kv cache so you have tighter CI. 
[06:33] Ethan Cole: Sounds good. Can you also break out the cost per 1M tokens for each config? 
[06:40] Maya Chen: Yes, that's in the spreadsheet. We'll surface a cost-per-token normalized to the same GPU pricing and also a unit cost when using QoS low-latency lanes. 
[06:50] Priya Singh: Any blockers from your side before we can proceed? 
[06:55] José Alvarez: We need the 500 sample requests and explicit SLOs to tune kv warm policies and QoS thresholds. Otherwise we can keep iterating on configs. 
[07:05] Priya Singh: We'll get those by Monday. 
[07:09] Maya Chen: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Redwood share cleaned spreadsheet + runbook + per-example diffs by 2025-03-07; SE to run 16-GPU throughput runs b=8 by 2025-03-09; Customer to share samples & SLOs by 2025-03-10; schedule infra deep-dive week of 2025-03-17. 
[07:28] Liam O'Neill: One last quick thing — can you include a short note on failure modes, e.g., fallback to smaller model if tail spikes? 
[07:36] José Alvarez: Yes, automatic fallback policies are part of the rollout: route to smaller model variant or stall to a warm cache. We'll document fallback logic. 
[07:47] Maya Chen: Awesome, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts. 
[07:52] Priya Singh: Thanks, bye. 
[07:55] End of call: 15:42 PST
